items.student_text: The line passes through several lattice points. Choose two points and calculate vertical change divided by horizontal change. Repeat with a different pair. What stays the same, and what does that number describe about the line?
items.answer_html: The ratio is 2 for any two points chosen in the same order. It describes a constant increase of 2 output units for each increase of 1 input unit.
items.solution_html: For example, using $(0,1)$ and $(2,5)$ gives $(5-1)/(2-0)=4/2=2$. Any other pair on this line gives the same slope.

items.answer_html: $A=4v+25$ and $B=9v$. Setting equal gives $25=5v$, so $v=5$. Before 5 visits, Plan B is cheaper; after 5 visits, Plan A is cheaper.

items.student_text: The scatter plot shows a clear upward trend, but the points do not lie exactly on one line. Explain why a linear model could still be useful. Name one prediction that would be interpolation and one that would be extrapolation.
items.answer_html: A line can summarize the overall trend even when individual data points vary. A prediction inside the observed input range is interpolation; a prediction beyond the observed range is extrapolation.

items.answer_html: $A=2.5r+30$, $B=5r$. Table: at 0, A=30 B=0; at 5, A=42.5 B=25; at 10, A=55 B=50; at 15, A=67.5 B=75. Equality: $2.5r+30=5r$, so $r=12$ and cost 60 dollars. B is cheaper below 12 riders; A is cheaper above 12. The intersection $(12,60)$ means both providers cost 60 dollars for 12 riders.

items.student_html:
Two community fitness plans use different pricing structures. Plan A charges a 36-dollar registration fee plus 4 dollars per visit. Plan B charges a 12-dollar registration fee plus 8 dollars per visit.
(a) Define a variable and write an equation for each plan.
(b) Make a table comparing the plans for 0, 3, 6, 9, and 12 visits.
(c) Find the number of visits where the plans cost the same and state the intersection as an ordered pair.
(d) A student says Plan B is always cheaper because it starts cheaper. Critique the claim using rate and starting-value evidence.
(e) Recommend a plan for a person expecting 4 visits and for a person expecting 12 visits. Support each recommendation with a calculated cost.
items.student_text: Two community fitness plans use different pricing structures. Plan A charges a 36-dollar registration fee plus 4 dollars per visit. Plan B charges a 12-dollar registration fee plus 8 dollars per visit. (a) Define a variable and write an equation for each plan. (b) Make a table comparing the plans for 0, 3, 6, 9, and 12 visits. (c) Find the number of visits where the plans cost the same and state the intersection as an ordered pair. (d) A student says Plan B is always cheaper because it starts cheaper. Critique the claim using rate and starting-value evidence. (e) Recommend a plan for a person expecting 4 visits and for a person expecting 12 visits. Support each recommendation with a calculated cost.
items.answer_html:
Let $v$ be visits. Plan A: $A=4v+36$. Plan B: $B=8v+12$.
Table values: at 0 visits A=36 B=12; 3 visits A=48 B=36; 6 visits A=60 B=60; 9 visits A=72 B=84; 12 visits A=84 B=108.
Equality: $4v+36=8v+12$, so $24=4v$ and $v=6$. The intersection is $(6,60)$.
The claim is false: Plan B starts 24 dollars lower but changes 4 dollars faster per visit, so it overtakes Plan A after 6 visits.
At 4 visits A=52 and B=44, so B is cheaper. At 12 visits A=84 and B=108, so A is cheaper.

items.student_html:
A class records practice time $x$ in hours and improvement score $y$: $(1,7)$, $(2,10)$, $(3,12)$, $(4,15)$, $(5,17)$, $(6,20)$.
(a) Organize the data in a table and describe the trend.
(b) Use the first and last points to build a reasonable linear model. Show the slope and intercept calculation.
(c) Use your model to predict the score at 4 hours and compare it with the observed value.
(d) Use the model to predict at 8 hours. Classify this as interpolation or extrapolation and explain one limitation.
(e) A second model is $y=4x+1$. Compare the two models using the data and decide which is more defensible for this set.
items.student_text: A class records practice time $x$ in hours and improvement score $y$: $(1,7)$, $(2,10)$, $(3,12)$, $(4,15)$, $(5,17)$, $(6,20)$. (a) Organize the data in a table and describe the trend. (b) Use the first and last points to build a reasonable linear model. Show the slope and intercept calculation. (c) Use your model to predict the score at 4 hours and compare it with the observed value. (d) Use the model to predict at 8 hours. Classify this as interpolation or extrapolation and explain one limitation. (e) A second model is $y=4x+1$. Compare the two models using the data and decide which is more defensible for this set.
items.answer_html:
The data increase roughly linearly. Using first and last points gives slope $(20-7)/(6-1)=13/5=2.6$. Using $(1,7)$ gives $7=2.6(1)+b$, so $b=4.4$. A reasonable model is $y=2.6x+4.4$.
At 4 hours the model predicts $14.8$, close to the observed 15. At 8 hours it predicts $25.2$; this is extrapolation because 8 lies beyond the observed range 1–6, so the trend may not continue unchanged.
The second model $y=4x+1$ gives predictions 5,9,13,17,21,25. It increasingly overshoots later data and has a much larger rate than the overall data. The $2.6x+4.4$ model is more defensible for this set.

At 4 hours the model predicts $14.8$, close to the observed 15. At 8 hours it predicts $25.2$; this is extrapolation because 8 lies beyond the observed range 1–6, so the trend may not continue unchanged.
